certifications_partner.text: , bulk cash, and other contraband concealed in hidden compartments within passenger vehicles, commercial trucks, tractor-trailers, and buses. Transnational criminal organizations continue to evolve their concealment methods, and Mexican federal, state, and military law enforcement personnel need specialized technical training, practical vehicle- inspection skills, and evidentiary-procedure knowledge to detect and disrupt these methods effectively. To meet this need, INL requires a contractor to deliver a phased, multi-year capacity-building program consisting of two distinct courses: (1) a Basic Interdiction and Hidden Compartment Certification course, to be delivered over the base year and option year one, providing foundational classroom and hands-on training using vehicles equipped with hidden compartments; and (2) a Train-the- Trainer course, to be delivered in option year two to previously certified participants, building an internal cadre of qualified Mexican instructors. The program also includes a follow-on Quality Control/Mentoring phase (option year three) to audit, mentor, and reinforce skills among trained personnel in the field. The contractor must be able to deliver training and mentoring both within Mexico and within the U.S., providing all required instruct

STATEMENT OF WORK ExCELS Capability: Building 333, Lab 123/114 Hardware/Interfacing 1.0 Introduction/Background: NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC) is developing the Experimental Communication and Electric Power for the Lunar Surface (ExCELS) capability to aid evaluating new technologies and addressing electrical power related issues. The goal is to create a flexible facility that allows for: i) addressing integration challenges as electric power technologies mature rather than addressing them later in the design process, ii) support mission studies and aid in developing system concept of operations, iii) test and V&V standards, specifications, and interface requirement documents, and iv) analyze unknown or boundary conditions. NASA GRC Power Facility in building 333 will host the High Voltage Development and Testing lab (lab 123) and the Real-time Modeling and High Voltage Control Lab (lab 114). The plan is to begin procurement of necessary equipment for hardware-in-the-loop testing capability development. 2.0 Scope of Work: This procurement is for (2) Yokogawa DL950 Oscilloscopes Specifications include: - Yokogawa Scopes: o 8 x 10MS/s 12bit Isolation Modules o NIST calibration service o Mathematics function, including motor control feature 3.0 Objectiv

PART 5 5.0 SPECIFIC TASKS 5.1 Basic Services: The contractor shall provide the following services: Graphic Designer (2 FTEs) Authored Works Review (Editor) (1 FTE) Writer and Author (Print Journalism) (1 FTE) Producer and Director (Video Production) (1 FTE) Public Relations Specialist (1 FTE) Executive Secretariat Program Manager - Publications & Issuances (1 FTE) 5.2 Special Qualifications: 5.2.1 When using education/certification in conjunction with labor categories, the COR in coordination with the CO must establish a review process of contractor personnel to ensure labor category requirements are met. 5.3 Summary of Qualifications and Duties 5.3.1 Graphic Designer (2 FTEs) Walter Reed National Military Medical Center is seeking two highly creative and strategically-minded Graphic Designers to serve as a primary visual storyteller for the nation's premier military medical center. This role is responsible for translating complex medical, military, and command information into compelling, high-impact visual communications. The ideal candidate will manage the entire l

the review and approval process for all video content, ensuring all stakeholders have provided input before final sign-off from the senior videographer and leadership. 5.3.5 Public Relations Specialist (1 FTE) Walter Reed is seeking a highly skilled Public Relations Specialist to lead strategic communication initiatives and manage high-impact projects. This hybrid role requires a professional who excels in crafting compelling messages, engaging diverse audiences, and ensuring communication projects are planned, executed, and delivered on time. The ideal candidate will have a strong background in public relations, project management with PMP certification, and a deep understanding of healthcare or public sector communications. Qualifications: Bachelor’s degree in communications, Public Relations, Project Management, or a related field. 5+ years of experience in public affairs, project management, or a combination of both roles. Strong written and verbal communication skills, with the ability to tailor messages to diverse audiences. Proven ability to manage multiple projects simultaneously in a fast-paced environment. Proficiency with project management tools and software, as well as digital communication tools. Familiarity with healthcare systems or military communications is highly desirable

PROJECT UNDERSTANDING Obstruction surveys for Army airfields use many of the same requirements as the other services; however, in some cases, the Army requirements differ and are more stringent in terms of identifying and reporting obstructions. One of the primary purposes of this document is to ensure that team members conducting obstruction surveys at Army airfields and the subsequent analysis are aware of these differing r equirements and adhere to them. The scheduling and review for Army airfield obstructions also follows a different process, so it is important to understand the roles, responsibilities and workflow for obstruction surveys at Army airfields. The US Army Aeronautical Services Agency (USAASA) serves as the functional proponent for Army airfields/heliports for Department of Army Headquarters and is the responsible official for airspace, aeronautical information, air traffic control, NOTAM and flight procedures policy. USAASA i

e and fund required obstruction surveys. Each Army airfield has an individual responsible for oversight and management of the airfield. Individuals in this role may have varying titles so this document will use the term “airfield manager” to reference the individual who is responsible for the airfield and is knowledgeable about the layout and operation of the airfield. The airfield manager is responsible for coordinating with the survey team. The US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) is the agency overseeing the project and can contract for this work. 2.2. PROJECT OVERVIEW 2.2.1. Project Start: Upon notice to proceed, the USACE project manager will schedule a kick-off meeting with the airfield manager , airfield's command representatives , USACE project team and survey team . The main purpose of this meeting is to introduce the survey team and airfield manager to facilitate coordination. 2.2.2. Pre-Survey Checklist: The survey team and the airfield manager should work together to complete the pre- survey check list in Appendix A prior to the start of field work. This is an important step that will ensure more productive field time. 2.2.3. Pre-Survey Research: The USACE project team will provide the deliverables from the most recent airfield survey if available. The

rdination with the airfield in preparation for the survey. To minimize costs, a reconnaissance trip is normally not used in these types of surveys. 5 2.2.4. Pre-Survey Report : Prior to mobilizing, the survey team shall send a brief pre- survey report. The purpose of this report is to identify any known or potenti al issues that could affect scope or duration of the field work. See Chapter 8 for report requirements. 2.2.5. Survey: The survey will be conducted in accordance with the criteria in this document and the scope of services. If there are any conflicts in guidance or criteria, they should be directed to the USACE project manager. A majority of Army airfield obstruction surveys over the past ten years have been entirely field surveyed. The use of aerial photography or aerial photography in conjunction with LiDAR may be approved on a case by case basis if a cost savings can be shown. Navigation aids (NAVAIDS) and runway features must be field surveyed in order to meet accuracy requir ements. Runway – A defined rectangular area prepared for the landing and takeoff run of aircraft along its length in a land airfield. Being exactly rectangular, it excludes narrow, rounded, deteriorated, and irregular ends that are not as wide as the general or overall width of the runway. The runway width is the physical width that extends over the entire length of the rectangle. The runway length does not include blast pad or clearzone surfaces. Displaced thresholds are APPENDIX H – Glossary of Airfield Features H-7 included in the physical length. Runways are normally numbered in relation to their magnetic direction rounded off to the nearest 10 degrees: e.g., Runway 10, Runway 25. Runway Centerline – A line connecting the two opposite runway end points. The line may be physically marked on the surface of the runway. Runway Centerline Reflectors (RWYCR) - Runway End Point – The point at the runway end halfway between the edges of the runway. Runway Length – The straight line (spatial) distance between runway end points. This line does not account for surface undulations between points. Offici

nated beginning of the runway. Touchdown Zone (TDZ) – The first 3,000 feet of the runway beginning at the threshold. Touchdown Zone Elevation (TDZE) – The highest elevation in the Touchdown Zone. Touchdown Reflector (TDR) - These reflectors work with either the Precision Approach Radar or the Ground Controlled Approach Radar to provide precision approach information for incoming aircraft. Transmissometer (TMOM) – An apparatus used to determine visibility by measuring the transmission of light through the atmosphere. It is the measurement source for determining runway visual range (RVR) and runway visibility value (RVV). APPENDIX H – Glossary of Airfield Features H-8 Transponder Landing System (TLS) – Transponder landing system providing azimuth and elevation guidance to aircraft on approach. Very High Frequency Omni-Directional Range Station (VOR) – A ground-based electronic navigation aid transmitting very high frequency navigation signals, 360 degrees in azimuth, referenced from magnetic north. Very High Frequency Omni-Directional Range/Tactical Air Navigation (VORTAC) – A navigation aid providing VOR azimuth, TACAN azimuth, and TACAN distance measuring equipment (DME) at one site. n closed network DoD systems. The scope of work includes: 1. Cabinet Enclosure 2. Advanced Cluster Technologies (ACT) Cluster Management Server 3. ACT Login Node Server 4. ACT Compute Nodes 5. ACT Scratch Storage Server 6. ACT Cold Storage Server 7. Administrative Network 8. Infiniband Fabric Network 9. ACT Cluster Management Software Suite 10. Complete system installation with interface to the existing power supply within a Top Secret facility 11. Maintenance and Warranty on all furnished equipment and software for a period of no less than 5 years from the time of installation 12. On-site training Detailed system specifications and minimum requirements for the HPC system are provided in the following sections. N0016726Q1092 Page 5 of 38 3.1 SYSTEM MINIMUM SPECIFICATIONS The ACT-brand HPC system shall be a commercially available system, production grade and scalable to meet future needs. The HPC system shall interface with facility and existing hardware and the existing power supply. The HPC system shall operate in the existing closed space with no modifications to the HVAC system or any ACT-brand other facility modification. The proximity of the system to the nearest HVAC register or return is not known. No circulating fan
